ukraine: Ukraine is the second-largest country in Europe after Russia and the largest entirely in Europe, covering 603,550 square kilometres with a coastline of 2,782 kilometres. It lies mostly in the East European Plain, and its landscape consists mostly of fertile steppes and plateaus crossed by rivers such as the Dnieper, the Dniester and the Southern Bug, which flow south to the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. The only mountains are the Carpathian Mountains in the west, of which the highest is Hoverla at 2,061 metres, and the Crimean Mountains in the extreme south. Significant natural resources include lithium, natural gas, kaolin, timber and abundant arable land.

Settlement by modern humans in Ukraine dates back to 32,000 BCE, and by 4,500 BCE the Neolithic Cucuteni–Trypillia culture was flourishing in wide areas. In the Iron Age the Cimmerians, Scythians and Sarmatians lived there. From the 6th century BCE Greek, Roman and Byzantine colonies such as Olbia and Chersonesus were established on the Black Sea shore. Kievan Rus' emerged in the 9th century, became the largest and most powerful realm in Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries, and was destroyed by the Mongols in the 13th century.

For the next 600 years the area was contested, divided and ruled by external powers including the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, the Kingdom of Poland, the Ottoman Empire and the Tsardom of Russia. The Cossack Hetmanate emerged in the 17th century and was gradually absorbed by the Russian Empire in the 18th century. The short-lived Ukrainian People's Republic was formed after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic became a constituent republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. In the early 1930s millions of Ukrainians died in the Holodomor, a human-made famine. During World War II Ukraine was occupied by Germany and endured major battles and atrocities, resulting in 7 million civilians killed, including most Ukrainian Jews.

Ukraine gained independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union dissolved, and adopted its constitution on 28 June 1996. Kyiv is the capital and largest city, and the official language is Ukrainian. The Orange Revolution of 2004 to 2005 and the Euromaidan of 2014 followed. Before 2022 the population was estimated at over 41 million.
ulaanbaatar: Ulaanbaatar lies at about 1,300 metres above sea level in a valley on the Tuul River, at the foot of Bogd Khan Mountain, which rises to 2,250 metres to the south and marks the boundary between the steppe zone and the forest-steppe zone to the north. Xiongnu-era royal tombs have been found around the city. Its elevation, latitude and distance from any coast make it the coldest national capital in the world.

The settlement began in 1639 as a yurt monastery called Örgöö, intended as the seat of Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu. It moved 29 times before it was permanently settled at its present site in 1778. By 1651 it was called Nomiin Khüree, and by 1706 Ikh Khüree. After the Treaty of Kyakhta in 1727 it became a major point of the Kyakhta trade between Russia and China, mostly Siberian furs for Chinese cloth and later tea.

In 1911, with the Qing dynasty collapsing, Mongolian leaders who had come to Ikh Khüree for Naadam met in secret on Mount Bogd Khan Uul and resolved to end 220 years of Manchu control. Soviet-style blocks of flats replaced most of the old ger districts from the 1950s, and the Trans-Mongolian Railway to Moscow and Beijing was completed in 1956. Most older temples and monasteries were destroyed in the purges of the late 1930s. Demonstrations in Sükhbaatar Square from 10 December 1989 led the governing party to resign on 9 March 1990, and a new constitution followed in 1992.

Ulaanbaatar is the capital and largest city of Mongolia, home to almost half of the country's population, and is governed as an independent first-level region separate from the surrounding Töv Province. It is divided into nine districts. The Choijin Lama Monastery, completed in 1908 and turned into a museum in 1942, and the Gandan Monastery, with its 26.5-metre statue of Migjid Janraisig, escaped the destruction of monasteries.
ulises-heureaux: Ulises Hilarión Heureaux Leibert, nicknamed Lilís, was born in Puerto Plata on 21 October 1845. His father, José D'Assás Heureaux Fortune, was born in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, the son of a judge of the civil court there and a member of his household staff; his mother, Josefa Leibert, was born on the island of Saint Thomas. He spoke French and English fluently as well as Spanish. In the rebellion that followed the Spanish annexation of 1861 he became the principal lieutenant of Gregorio Luperón. In 1876 he organised an uprising that seized Puerto Plata and led to the election of Ulises Espaillat.

When Luperón became president in 1879 and stayed in Puerto Plata, he delegated authority in Santo Domingo to Heureaux. Under the priest Fernando Meriño, president from September 1880, Heureaux was interior minister, and Meriño handed the government to him on 1 September 1882. In 1884 Luperón backed General Segundo Imbert as successor; Heureaux promised to respect the result but had ballot boxes stuffed for General Francisco Gregorio Billini. Billini was driven to resign on 16 May 1885. In the 1886 election the fraud committed by Heureaux was so blatant that supporters of his opponent, Casimiro de Moya, rose in the Cibao Valley, and he suppressed the rising brutally.

In 1888 he exiled Luperón, and the next year he forced Congress to abolish the bar on presidential re-election and to end direct elections. He brought members of both rival factions, the Rojos and the Azules, into his government, and kept an extensive network of secret police and informants, assassinating or exiling the politicians he could not co-opt. Cuban planters who arrived after the Ten Years' War received large tracts of the southeastern coastal plain and built the country's first mechanised sugar mills. His government electrified Santo Domingo, bridged the Ozama River and began a railway from Santiago to Puerto Plata.

In 1888 he borrowed three-quarters of a million pounds sterling from the Amsterdam house of Westendorp, which went bankrupt in 1892. The San Domingo Improvement Co. of New York bought out its claims. In 1897, with the country near bankruptcy, he printed five million dollars of unsecured paper money, the papeletas de Lilís, which ruined many merchants and helped to provoke a revolt among the tobacco planters and merchants of the Cibao. He was killed by Ramón Cáceres on 26 July 1899. The national debt then exceeded 35 million dollars, fifteen times the annual budget; the government declared bankruptcy, and the American military intervened.
ulugh-khan: Ulugh Khan was originally named Almas Beg. His father, Shihabuddin Mas'ud, was the elder brother of Sultan Jalaluddin, founder of the Khalji dynasty, and both Almas Beg and his elder brother Alauddin married daughters of Jalaluddin. Under Jalaluddin he held the post of Akhur-beg, equivalent to master of the horse. In 1296, after Alauddin had raided Devagiri and kept the loot, Almas Beg assured the sultan of his brother's loyalty and persuaded him to visit Kara, where Alauddin killed him on 20 July 1296. The new sultan made his brother barbeg with the title Ulugh Khan, meaning Great Khan. He also held the iqta' of Bayana.

In November 1296 Alauddin sent him and Zafar Khan with an army of 30,000 to 40,000 against Multan, held by Jalaluddin's son Arkali Khan. After two months of siege the leaders of the defence went over to Delhi. Ulugh Khan promised Arkali Khan and his brother Ruknuddin Ibrahim that they would not be harmed, but imprisoned them once the city was occupied; they were later blinded or killed by Nusrat Khan on Alauddin's orders. According to the courtier Amir Khusrau, he reached the Sutlej River on 6 February 1298 and defeated the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate there, with 20,000 Mongol dead.

On the way back from Gujarat in 1299, near Jalore, he and Nusrat Khan punished soldiers for withholding the khums, the fifth of the loot due to the treasury. Recently converted Mongol soldiers mutinied; some 2,000 to 3,000 attacked his camp and killed a nephew of Alauddin whom they took for him. Against Hammira of Ranthambore in 1301 he defeated and killed the general Bhimasimha at the Banas River, but after Nusrat Khan was killed in the siege he was forced back to Jhain, and Alauddin came in person and took the fort in July 1301.

Ordered to prepare a march on the Kakatiya capital Warangal, he assembled a large army but died a few months later. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani writes that Alauddin was greatly depressed and gave much in charity for his brother's soul. Barani's contemporary Isami claims instead that Alauddin had him poisoned, suspecting that he had been ready to take the throne when the sultan was wrongly reported dead; later chroniclers repeat this. The historian Banarsi Prasad Saksena dismisses Isami's account as false, while Kishori Saran Lal thinks it not impossible. Claims that he led the invasion of Gujarat in 1304, or governed it for 20 years, are of doubtful accuracy.
ulysses-s-grant: Grant was born Hiram Ulysses Grant on 27 April 1822, the first child of Jesse Root Grant, a Whig supporter and fervent abolitionist, and Hannah Simpson. The family moved to Georgetown, Ohio, in 1823. When Representative Thomas L. Hamer nominated him to the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1839, Hamer altered his name, and he was enlisted as U. S. Grant. He served in the Mexican–American War and married Julia Dent on 22 August 1848. After resigning in 1854 he had no trade, and seven years of financial struggle followed; he farmed near St. Louis and sold firewood on its street corners.

When the Civil War began in April 1861 Grant became colonel of the 21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment. His victories in the western theatre in 1862 brought him prominence, and in 1863 his Vicksburg campaign gave Union forces control of the Mississippi River. After Chattanooga, Abraham Lincoln promoted him to lieutenant general and command of all Union armies. Grant fought Robert E. Lee through the Overland Campaign in 1864, and a nine-month siege of Petersburg followed. Lee abandoned Petersburg and Richmond after a general assault ordered on 2 April 1865 and surrendered at Appomattox.

Nominated unanimously by the Republicans in 1868, Grant was sworn in as president on 4 March 1869 and urged ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment. He appointed Ely S. Parker, a Seneca, as Commissioner of Indian Affairs, the first Native American in the post. His second term was beset by scandals, and the Panic of 1873 began the Long Depression. Leaving office in 1877, he toured the world for about two and a half years, meeting Queen Victoria, Otto von Bismarck, Li Hongzhang and Emperor Meiji.

Grant failed to win the Republican nomination for a third term in 1880. His savings were depleted, and a railway venture in Mexico went bankrupt in 1884. That autumn he learned that a sore throat was cancer, possibly caused by his frequent cigar smoking, and he wrote his memoirs as he was dying. He died on 23 July 1885. At his death he was the most popular American and was memorialised as a symbol of national unity. His reputation suffered for a time under the Lost Cause mythology spread by Confederate sympathisers around the turn of the twentieth century.
umar-marvi: The tale is said to date back to the 14th century and probably originated in the Soomra period, between 1050 and 1350. It was first written down in the 16th century by Shah Abdul Karim of Bulri, the great-great-grandfather of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, in his Bayan ul Arifeen, known to Sindhis as Karim Jo Risalo. It also appears in two chronicles, the Tarikh-i Tahiri, compiled in 1621, and the Tuhfat-al-Kiram of 1766–67.

In the story as it is told, Marvi is a young Khaskheli girl of the Panhwar tribe, and her captor is Umar Soomro, then ruler of Umerkot, who wanted to marry her for her beauty. When she refused him she was held for several years in Umarkot Fort. She resists both the ruler's overtures and the temptation to live in the palace as a queen, preferring a simple rural life among her own village people.

In the Shah Jo Risalo the tale stands among seven popular tragic romances of Sindh, with Sassui Punnhun, Sohni Mehar, Lilan Chanesar, Noori Jam Tamachi, Sorath Rai Diyach and Momal Rano. Their heroines are commonly known as the Seven Queens of Sindh, or the seven heroines of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Marvi is regarded, for her courage, as a symbol of love for one's soil.

The story has been retold in modern forms. A film, Umar Marvi, directed by Shaikh Hassan and produced by Syed Hussain Ali Shah Fazlani, who also acted in it, was released on 12 March 1956 as the first Sindhi-language feature film made in Pakistan. The Pakistan Television Corporation broadcast a serial, Marvi, in 1993, which set the story in modern times. The Indian writer Ram Panjwani wrote a Sindhi play, Umar Marui, and a Sindhi song of Coke Studio's fifteenth season, Aayi Aayi, was inspired by the tale.
unesco: The organisation's mandate for international cooperation can be traced to a League of Nations resolution of 21 September 1921, which asked for a commission to study whether nations could freely share cultural, educational and scientific achievements. The resulting International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation was created in 1922. Its members included Henri Bergson, Albert Einstein, Marie Curie, Robert A. Millikan and Gonzague de Reynold, and it was a small body centred largely on Western Europe.

The International Institute for Intellectual Cooperation was set up in Paris in September 1924 as the committee's executing agency. The International Bureau of Education began work in December 1925 as a non-governmental body; it formed a joint commission with UNESCO in 1952 and joined it in 1969. World War II largely interrupted the work of the predecessor bodies, and UNESCO was founded in 1945 as their successor.

UNESCO is governed by a General Conference of member states and associate members, which meets every two years to set its programmes and budget. The conference elects an executive board of 58 members who hold office for four years, and appoints a Director-General every four years. The headquarters stand at the Place de Fontenoy in Paris, built by a group of architects including Bernard Zehrfuss, Marcel Breuer and Luigi Nervi. The grounds hold a Garden of Peace, given by the government of Japan and designed by Isamu Noguchi in 1958.

Its work falls under five programme areas: education, natural sciences, social and human sciences, culture, and communication and information. It adopted the Convention against Discrimination in Education in 1960 and the Seville Statement on Violence in 1989, and it designates places and projects of significance, among them biosphere reserves, begun in 1971, and the Memory of the World register, begun in 1997.

In the 1970s and 1980s UNESCO's support for a New World Information and Communication Order was condemned in the United States, the United Kingdom and Singapore as an attempt to curb freedom of the press. The United States withheld its contributions and withdrew in 1984, and the United Kingdom followed in 1985. Singapore also left at the end of 1985, citing rising membership fees. The United Kingdom rejoined after a change of government in 1997, the United States in 2003 and Singapore on 8 October 2007.
unesco-world-heritage-site: The programme grew out of a rescue operation. In 1954 the government of Egypt decided to build the Aswan High Dam, whose reservoir would flood a stretch of the Nile valley containing the cultural treasures of ancient Egypt and ancient Nubia. In 1960 UNESCO's Director-General launched the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia, which led to the excavation and recording of hundreds of sites and the relocation of several temples, among them Abu Simbel and Philae. Its success led to campaigns for Venice, the ruins of Mohenjo-daro and the Borobodur Temple Compounds.
The Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted by the General Conference of UNESCO on 16 November 1972 and came into force on 17 December 1975.

A site is nominated by its host country and decided on by UNESCO's World Heritage Committee, whose 21 states parties are elected by the United Nations General Assembly. A country first lists its sites on a Tentative List and then submits a Nomination File, evaluated by the International Council on Monuments and Sites and the World Conservation Union. A site must be of outstanding universal value and meet at least one of ten criteria.

A site may be placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger when threats such as armed conflict, pollution or uncontrolled development endanger it. Three sites have been removed from the list altogether: the Arabian Oryx Sanctuary in Oman in 2007, the Dresden Elbe Valley in Germany in 2009 and Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City in 2021.

A listed site gains international recognition and legal protection and can obtain money from the World Heritage Fund. UNESCO counts the restorations of Angkor, the Old City of Dubrovnik, the Wieliczka Salt Mine and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area among its successes. The programme has also drawn criticism for the under-representation of sites outside Europe, for disputed selections, and for the effects of mass tourism.
united-nations: In the century before its creation, bodies such as the International Committee of the Red Cross were formed to protect and assist victims of armed conflict. During the First World War several leaders, above all the American president Woodrow Wilson, advocated a world body to guarantee peace, and the League of Nations came into being on 10 January 1920 when its Covenant, ratified by 42 nations in 1919, took effect.

The United States never joined. Most of the League's substantive decisions required unanimity, and it failed to act against Japan in Manchuria and against Italy in the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, despite the appeal of Emperor Haile Selassie I at Geneva in 1936. It effectively closed down when the Second World War broke out in 1939. The United Nations was established by the signing of its Charter on 26 June 1945.

The UN has six principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council, which suspended its work on 1 November 1994 on the independence of Palau, the last trust territory. The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague, and the other organs have their main seat in New York City, with major offices at Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. Its six official languages are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.

Membership has 193 states, the most recent being South Sudan, which joined on 14 July 2011; the Holy See and Palestine are observer states. Indonesia is the only state to have tried to withdraw, in 1965, and it resumed membership in 1966. Because the UN keeps no military of its own, peacekeepers are provided voluntarily by member states and approved by the Security Council. The UN has carried out 71 peacekeeping operations since 1947, and its Truce Supervision Organization has been in the Middle East since 1948.

Peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988, and the UN and Kofi Annan shared it in 2001. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees won it in 1954 and 1981. Political scientists such as Virginia Page Fortna have found that UN-led conflict resolution usually resulted in long-term peace, while critics describe the Security Council veto as undemocratic and a main cause of inaction on genocides. There is also a divide between richer Northern and developing Southern states over how strong the UN should be. A Hymn to the United Nations, with words by W. H. Auden, was performed by Pau Casals on 24 October 1971.
united-states: The United States is the third or fourth largest country by total area, with figures ranging between 9,629,091 and 9,866,624 square kilometres. The coastal plain of the Atlantic seaboard gives way to the Piedmont plateau, and the Appalachian Mountains separate the East Coast from the Great Lakes and the grasslands of the Midwest. The Mississippi River System runs north to south through the centre of the country, the Great Plains stretch to the west, and the Rocky Mountains extend across the country beyond them. Alaska is a semi-exclave whose Denali, at 6,190 metres, is the highest peak in the country, while the Hawaiian archipelago lies entirely outside North America.

The first inhabitants of North America migrated from Siberia at least 15,000 years ago. The Clovis culture, which appeared around 11,000 BCE, is believed to be the first widespread culture in the Americas, and later the Mississippian culture developed agriculture, architecture and complex societies. Estimates of the native population before the arrival of European colonizers range from around 500,000 to nearly 10 million. Spain chartered Spanish Florida in 1513 and founded Saint Augustine in 1565. France, the Dutch colony of New Nederland and the Swedish colony of New Sweden also settled parts of the continent, and British colonization began with the Virginia Colony in 1607 and the Plymouth Colony in 1620.

Clashes with the British Crown over taxation without parliamentary representation sparked the American Revolution. Independence was formally declared in the Lee Resolution of 2 July 1776, two days before the Declaration of Independence, and victory in the Revolutionary War of 1775 to 1783 confirmed international recognition. The country expanded westward through purchase, settlement and conquest. A sectional division over slavery led 11 Southern states to secede and form the Confederate States of America, which fought the Union in the Civil War of 1861 to 1865. Slavery was abolished after the Union's victory.

The United States is a federal republic of 50 states and a federal capital district. Its Constitution created a separation of powers among legislative, executive and judicial branches. Congress consists of the Senate, with 100 members, and the House of Representatives, with 435 voting members. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of the population was 341,784,857. About 82% of Americans live in metropolitan areas. By 1900 the country had emerged as a great power.
universal-declaration-of-human-rights: During the Second World War the Allies, formally known as the United Nations, adopted the Four Freedoms as their basic war aims: freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom from want and freedom from fear. The United Nations Charter reaffirmed faith in fundamental human rights, but when the atrocities of Nazi Germany became fully apparent after the war, the world community judged that the Charter did not sufficiently define the rights it referred to. A declaration that specified the rights of individuals was thought necessary to give effect to its provisions.

In June 1946 the Economic and Social Council created the Commission on Human Rights, with 18 members of varied national, religious and political backgrounds. In February 1947 the Commission set up a Drafting Committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt of the United States. The Canadian John Peters Humphrey, Director of the Division of Human Rights in the UN Secretariat, became the principal drafter. P. C. Chang of China was vice-chairman, René Cassin of France prepared the second draft, and Charles Malik of Lebanon was rapporteur. The committee was soon enlarged to include Australia, Chile, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom, and it met in two sessions over two years.

The structure of the Declaration, a preamble followed by general principles, was influenced by the Code Napoléon. Articles 1 and 2 establish dignity, liberty and equality for all humans. Articles 3 to 5 deal with the right to life and the prohibition of slavery and torture, and articles 6 to 11 with legal remedies when rights are violated. Articles 12 to 17 cover the individual's rights towards the community, including freedom of movement, property, nationality and asylum, and articles 18 to 21 the freedoms of thought, conscience, religion, expression and assembly. Articles 22 to 27 set out economic, social and cultural rights, among them work, health, housing and education, and articles 28 to 30 describe how the rights are to be exercised and their limits.

The General Assembly adopted the Declaration on 10 December 1948. Roosevelt told it that the text was not a treaty or a statement of legal obligation but a declaration of basic principles, a common standard of achievement for all peoples. It remains non-binding, yet it was the first step towards the International Bill of Human Rights, completed in 1966 and in force from 1976, and its contents have been elaborated in later treaties, regional instruments and national constitutions.

The Declaration was officially adopted as a French document, with official translations in English, Chinese, Russian and Spanish. It has been translated into more languages than any other document: 298 translations when the Guinness Book of Records recorded the fact in 1999, and more than 500 by 2016.
urdu: Urdu is an Indo-Aryan language that originated in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab, in and around the Delhi region, where Khari Boli was spoken. It shared a grammatical foundation with Khari Boli but was written in a revised Perso-Arabic script and borrowed vocabulary from Persian and Arabic. The contact of Hindu and Muslim cultures during the Muslim conquests of the twelfth to sixteenth centuries led to Hindustani, a product of what is called a composite Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.

Amir Khusrau, called the father of Urdu literature, founded an early literary tradition of Hindavi in the late thirteenth century. After the conquest of the Deccan, a form called Dakhini flourished as a vehicle of poetry, especially under the Bahmanids, with loanwords from Telugu and Marathi. The poet Ghulam Hamadani Mushafi used the name Urdu around 1780; ordu means army in Turkic languages.

Urdu is closely related to Hindi. They share a vocabulary base largely derived from Sanskrit and Prakrit, and the same phonology, syntax and grammar, so that many linguists count them as one language, Hindustani. Formal Urdu takes its literary and technical vocabulary from Persian and Arabic, formal Hindi from Sanskrit. Urdu is written right to left in an extension of the Persian alphabet, in the Nastaʿlīq style of calligraphy, and because Nastaʿlīq has thousands of ligatures, Urdu newspapers were handwritten by calligraphers until the late 1980s.

In 1837 Urdu became an official language of the British East India Company, replacing Persian across northern India; Persian had until then been the court language of the Indo-Islamic empires. In the early nineteenth century religious and social divisions led Urdu and Hindi to be set apart as distinct identities, associated with Muslims and Hindus respectively, each with its own script.

Urdu was chosen as a symbol of unity for the new Dominion of Pakistan in 1947, having already served as a lingua franca among Muslims in the north and northwest of British India. It is the national language of Pakistan, and in India it is among the languages of the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
uruguay: Uruguay covers about 176,214 square kilometres of continental land and is the second-smallest sovereign nation in South America, after Suriname. The landscape is mostly rolling plains and low hill ranges called cuchillas, with a fertile coastal lowland and 660 kilometres of coastline. The highest point is Cerro Catedral, at 514 metres. The Río de la Plata lies to the south-west, and the Río Negro, dammed in 1945, formed the artificial Rincón del Bonete Lake. Montevideo is the southernmost national capital in the Americas, and Uruguay lies entirely south of the Tropic of Capricorn.

Hunter-gatherers lived in the region about 13,000 years ago. At the first contact with Europeans in the 16th century there were an estimated 9,000 Charrúa and 6,000 Chaná, with some Guaraní island settlements. Eastern Uruguay holds man-made tumuli called Cerritos de Indios, some about 5,000 years old. The Portuguese entered the region in 1512, and the Spanish in 1515. Fierce resistance and the lack of valuable resources limited settlement, the Spanish introduced cattle in 1603, and the first permanent Spanish settlement was Soriano in 1624. The Portuguese built a fort at Colonia del Sacramento in 1680, and the Spanish founded Montevideo in 1726 as a military stronghold.

British forces occupied Montevideo from February to September 1807. In 1811 José Gervasio Artigas, later Uruguay's national hero, led a revolt against Spanish authority and won the Battle of Las Piedras on 18 May. He became a champion of federalism and demanded autonomy for the Banda Oriental, while Buenos Aires pursued unitary centralism. Independence was secured between 1811 and 1828, after a struggle involving Portugal, Spain, the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and the Empire of Brazil, and a constitution was enacted in 1830.

From the second half of the 19th century migration from Spain, Italy and France reshaped the population, and in the 20th century Uruguay became an advanced welfare state nicknamed the Switzerland of the Americas. Tensions during the Cold War, including the activities of the Tupamaros urban guerrilla movement, eroded democratic institutions, and a coup in 1973 began a dictatorship that lasted until 1985.

Uruguay is now a constitutional republic with a presidential system. Its 1967 constitution allows citizens to propose bills and call referendums, a feature drawn from Switzerland. Montevideo's metropolitan area holds about 1.9 million of its almost 3.5 million people, and 86.0 per cent identified as white in the 2023 census.
utah: Utah is a landlocked state in the Mountain West and one of the Four Corners states, sharing a border with Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico, and also bordering Wyoming, Idaho and Nevada. It lies at the convergence of three geological regions: the Rocky Mountains, the Great Basin and the Colorado Plateau. Most of the western half lies in the Great Basin. The Wasatch Range runs down the middle of the northern third, and the Uinta Mountains in the northeast hold Kings Peak, the highest point. At the western base of the Wasatch Range lies the Wasatch Front, a series of valleys and basins stretching from Brigham City to Nephi, where about 75 per cent of the population lives.

The Ancestral Puebloans and the Fremont people lived in Utah for thousands of years before Europeans arrived; the Fremont built houses of straw and disappeared from the region around the 15th century. The Navajo settled in the region around the 18th century, and in the mid-18th century the Goshute, Paiute, Shoshone and Ute also settled there. The name Utah comes from the Spanish Yuta, recorded from the 17th century and borrowed from the name of the Ute, a people whose name for themselves is Núuchi-u. It is commonly said to mean people of the mountains.

Francisco Vázquez de Coronado explored southern Utah in 1540 while looking for Cíbola. A group led by two Catholic priests, the Domínguez-Escalante expedition, left Santa Fe in 1776 hoping to find a route to California and travelled as far north as Utah Lake. In 1821, the year Mexico became independent, the region became part of its territory of Alta California.

Many early settlers, even under Mexico, came from the United States, among them Mormons fleeing persecution. In 1848, after the Mexican-American War, the region was annexed by the United States and became Utah Territory. Disputes between the Mormon community and Congress delayed statehood until 1896, when, after Utah agreed to outlaw polygamy, it was admitted as the 45th state.

The capital is Salt Lake City, on the Wasatch Front. The 2020 census counted 3,271,616 people. Slightly over half of Utahns are Mormons, mostly members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which has its world headquarters in Salt Lake City, and Utah is the only state where a majority belongs to a single church.
uzbekistan: Uzbekistan has an area of 448,978 square kilometres and stretches 1,425 kilometres from west to east. It is doubly landlocked: none of its rivers reach the sea, since they lie in a series of endorheic basins. It is the only Central Asian state that borders all four of the others. Less than 10% of its territory is intensively cultivated irrigated land in river valleys and oases, and the rest is the vast Kyzylkum Desert and mountains. The climate is continental, with 100 to 200 millimetres of precipitation a year. The highest point is Khazret Sultan at 4,643 metres. The Aral Sea has been largely desiccated by cotton production established in the Soviet era.

During early antiquity the region was inhabited by nomadic Scythian tribes, who built an extensive irrigation system along the rivers when they settled, and cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand emerged as centres of government and high culture. By the fifth century BCE the Bactrian, Sogdian and Tokharian states dominated the region. Sogdian intermediaries became the wealthiest intermediaries in the silk trade between East Asia and the West, which made Bukhara and Samarkand extremely wealthy. Cyrus the Great and later Darius the Great incorporated Bactria and Chorasmia as satrapies, and in 327 BCE Alexander the Great conquered Sogdiana and Bactria, meeting fierce popular resistance. The Kushan Empire replaced the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom in the first century BCE.

In the eighth century the Arabs under Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Transoxiana, the land between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, which soon became a focal point of the Islamic Golden Age. The Mongol invasion of the 13th century destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire, and in the 14th century Timur established the Timurid Empire from here. Samarkand became a centre of science under Ulugh Beg. Turko-Mongol Shaybanids conquered the Timurid lands in the 16th century, and most of Central Asia was gradually incorporated into the Russian Empire in the 19th, with Tashkent the political centre of Russian Turkestan. The Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1924, and independence was declared in 1991.

Uzbekistan is a secular state with a semi-presidential government, made up of 12 regions, Tashkent City and the autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan. Uzbek is the official language and Russian serves as a lingua franca, while Tajik is spoken mainly in the south around Samarkand and Bukhara. Uzbeks form more than 89% of the population, and most people are Muslim. Many of the great monuments of the Timurid period survive in Samarkand. Uzbekistan is a member of the United Nations and the Commonwealth of Independent States.
